ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: In real life, we often see many "standard" rectangles, such as the covers of our textbooks, A4 printing paper, etc. In fact, the ratio of the length to the width of these rectangles is $\sqrt{2}: 1$. We might as well call such rectangles "standard rectangles". In the "standard rectangle" $ABCD$, as shown in the figure, point $Q$ is on $DC$, and $DQ=AD$. If $G$ is a moving point on side $BC$, when the perimeter of $\triangle AGQ$ is minimized, what is the value of $\frac{CG}{GB}$?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} Let DC=$\sqrt{2}x$, DQ=AD=$x$,\\
$\therefore$ $CQ=(\sqrt{2}-1)x$\\
$\because$ In rectangle ABCD,\\
$\therefore$ $\angle D=\angle DCB=\angle B=90^\circ$, $AB=DC=\sqrt{2}x$, $BC=AD=x$,\\
$\therefore$ $AQ=\sqrt{AD^2+DQ^2}=\sqrt{2}x$,\\
As shown in the figure, construct the symmetric point E of point Q with respect to BC, and connect AE to intersect BC at point M,\\
$\therefore$ GQ=GE, CQ=CE=$(\sqrt{2}-1)x$\\
$\therefore$ AQ+QG+AG=$\sqrt{2}x+AG+EG\ge \sqrt{2}x+AE$,\\
$\therefore$ When points A, G, and E are collinear, the perimeter of $\triangle AGQ$ is minimized,\\
At this time, point G should be located at point M in the figure;\\
$\because$ In rectangle ABCD, $\angle QCG=90^\circ$,\\
$\therefore$ Point E lies on the extension line of QC,\\
$\therefore$ CE$\parallel$AB,\\
$\therefore$ $\frac{CM}{MB}=\frac{CE}{AB}=\frac{(\sqrt{2}-1)x}{\sqrt{2}x}=\frac{2-\sqrt{2}}{2}$,\\
which means $\frac{CG}{GB}=\boxed{\frac{2-\sqrt{2}}{2}}$.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the attached figure is rectangle ABCD, A is at the lower left, B is at the lower right, C is at the upper right, D is at the upper left; Q is on the upper side DC, G is on the right side BC; in the figure AQ, QG, AG are connected, forming triangle AGQ. Reasoning: Let the short side of the standard rectangle AD=BC=x, and the long side DC=AB=√2x. Establish a coordinate system: A=(0,0), B=(√2x,0), C=(√2x,x), D=(0,x). Because DQ=AD=x and Q is on DC, Q=(x,x). Let G=(√2x,y), where 0≤y≤x, then GB=y, CG=x−y. The perimeter of triangle AGQ is AQ+AG+GQ, where AQ=√(x²+x²)=√2x is a constant, so it is only necessary to minimize f(y)=AG+GQ=√(2x²+y²)+√((√2−1)²x²+(y−x)²). Differentiating gives f'(y)=y/√(2x²+y²)+(y−x)/√((√2−1)²x²+(y−x)²). Let f'(y)=0, then y/√(2x²+y²)=(x−y)/√((√2−1)²x²+(x−y)²). Squaring and simplifying: y²(√2−1)²x²=2x²(x−y)², so (√2−1)y=√2(x−y). Thus √2x=(2√2−1)y, hence y=√2x/(2√2−1). Therefore CG/GB=(x−y)/y=x/y−1=(2√2−1)/√2−1=(√2−1)/√2=(2−√2)/2.
